text: Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and on to the border of Egypt. They brought tribute and served Solomon all the days of his life.
Solomon's provisions for a single day were thirty kors of fine flour and sixty kors of meal,
ten fattened oxen, twenty pasture-fed cattle, and a hundred sheep and goats, besides deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened fowl.
For he held sway over the whole region west of the Euphrates, from Tiphsah to Gaza, and over all its kings, and he had peace on every side.

versions.text: For he held sway over the whole region west of the Euphrates, from Tiphsah to Gaza, over all the kings west of the River, and he had peace on every side.
versions.explanation: The same Hebrew phrase (עֵבֶר הַנָּהָר) is rendered two different ways in one verse ("west of the Euphrates" / "west of the River"), which sounds repetitive and slightly confusing when read aloud. Condensing the second occurrence keeps the meaning and improves rhythm.

text: So Judah and Israel lived in safety, everyone under his own vine and his own fig tree, from Dan to Beersheba, all the days of Solomon.
Solomon had forty thousand stalls of horses for his chariots and twelve thousand horsemen.
Those officers supplied provisions for King Solomon and for all who came to King Solomon's table, each in his appointed month; they let nothing be lacking.
They also brought barley and straw for the horses and the swift steeds to the place where they were needed, each according to his assigned duty.

versions.text: They also brought barley and straw for the chariot horses and the swift steeds to whatever place he was, each according to his assignment.
versions.explanation: "to whatever place he was" is ungrammatical and unclear in English (a missing relative pronoun, and an ambiguous "he"). The Hebrew means the supplies were delivered to the place where they were required. The revision reads smoothly aloud and preserves the sense of each officer fulfilling his appointed obligation.

versions.text: They also brought barley and straw for the chariot horses and the swift steeds to the place where they were needed, each according to his assigned duty.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew סוּסִים simply means "horses"; the qualifier "chariot" is an added specification not present in the text, and it also blurs the distinction with רָכֶשׁ ("swift steeds"), which is the term more often associated with chariotry. Dropping "chariot" is both more accurate and slightly tighter for reading aloud.

text: God gave Solomon wisdom and very great insight, and a breadth of understanding as measureless as the sand on the seashore.
Solomon's wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the peoples of the East and all the wisdom of Egypt.
He was wiser than anyone else—wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and than Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol—and his fame spread through all the surrounding nations.
He composed three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered a thousand and five.
He spoke about trees, from the cedar of Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of a wall; and he spoke about animals and birds, creeping things and fish.
People came from every nation to hear Solomon's wisdom, sent by all the kings of the earth who had heard how wise he was.
When Hiram king of Tyre heard that Solomon had been anointed king in place of his father, he sent his servants to him, for Hiram had always been a friend of David.
And Solomon sent this message to Hiram:

"You know that my father David could not build a house for the name of the LORD his God because of the wars that surrounded him on every side, until the LORD put his enemies under the soles of my feet.
But now the LORD my God has given me rest on every side; there is no adversary, no disaster.
So I intend to build a house for the name of the LORD my God, just as the LORD told my father David: 'Your son, whom I will set on your throne in your place, he shall build the house for my name.'

Now then, give orders that cedars of Lebanon be cut for me. My servants will work alongside your servants, and I will pay you whatever wages you set for your servants. For you know that we have no one who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians."
When Hiram heard Solomon's message, he was overjoyed and said, "Blessed be the LORD this day, who has given David a wise son to rule this great people."
So Hiram sent word to Solomon: "I have received your message. I will do everything you desire with the cedar and cypress timber.

My servants will bring the logs down from Lebanon to the sea, and I will float them in rafts by sea to the place you designate. There I will have them broken apart, and you can take them away. And you, in turn, will meet my need by supplying food for my household."
So Hiram kept Solomon supplied with all the cedar and cypress timber he wanted,
and Solomon gave Hiram twenty thousand kors of wheat as food for his household and twenty kors of pressed oil. This Solomon gave to Hiram year after year.
The LORD gave Solomon wisdom, just as he had promised him. There was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty.
King Solomon conscripted laborers from all Israel—thirty thousand men in all.
He sent them to Lebanon in shifts of ten thousand a month, so that they spent one month in Lebanon and two months at home. Adoniram was in charge of the forced labor.
Solomon also had seventy thousand men to carry loads and eighty thousand to quarry stone in the hills,
besides his three thousand three hundred foremen who were in charge of the project and supervised the workers.
At the king's command they quarried huge, costly blocks of dressed stone to lay the foundation of the temple.
Solomon's builders and Hiram's builders, together with the men of Gebal, cut and shaped them, and they prepared the timber and the stone for building the temple.
